Grade 3 ABRSM violin is the gateway between "beginner who can play tunes" and "real student". Two new flat keys appear (B♭ and E♭), the three minor scales must be distinguished, a hint of position shifting is introduced, and bowings begin to diversify (slurred staccato, hooked bowing). The repertoire shifts toward Baroque dances and early Classical pieces.
Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → 02 Grade 2 → 03 Grade 3 (this post) → 04 Grade 4 → … → 08 Grade 8.

Play two-octave scales of G, D, A, B♭ majors and one-octave E♭ major.
Play D, G, A natural and harmonic minors (one or two octaves as syllabus).
Distinguish the three minor forms by ear and on paper.
Use slurred staccato and hooked bowing.
Prepare for 3rd position shifting (theoretical introduction).
Identify interval quality (major, minor, perfect) at sight.
Play 5–7 Grade 3 pieces with confident phrasing.

B♭ has two flats: B♭ and E♭. Translated to violin fingering:
G string: G 1=A 2=B♭(low 2!) 3=C
D string: D 1=E♭(low 1!) 2=F 3=G
A string: A 1=B♭(low 1!) 2=C 3=D 4=E♭(low 4!)
E string: (open E not used) 1=F 2=G 3=A 4=B♭(low 4!)
Wait — that's a lot of "low" fingers across the scale: every B♭ and E♭, plus F and G on the E string. The hand shape changes per string.
Trick: the rule for any key with flats: drop the finger that plays the flatted note half a finger-width toward the nut. For B♭ major, that's 2 on G string, 1 on D, 1 and 4 on A, 4 on E. Memorise the pattern of which finger is low, not the abstract scale.
Top note: B♭5 (4th finger on E in 1st position).
B♭ is the first key violinists genuinely struggle with. The hand has to relearn its default spacing. Master B♭ by Grade 3, and every flat key after becomes intuitive.

E♭ has three flats: B♭, E♭, A♭. One octave only at Grade 3.
D string: 1=E♭(low 1!) 2=F 3=G 4=A♭(low 4!)
A string: 1=B♭(low 1!) 2=C 3=D 4=E♭(low 4!)
E string: not needed — one octave stops at E♭5 (4th finger on A)
Fingerings vary a little between editions. The point: 3 flats means every B♭, E♭ and A♭ gets a "low" finger. Get the pattern of lowness right and your fingers will land.
Where I got stuck: I tried to memorise E♭ as "B♭, E♭, A♭" abstractly. Fix: I stopped naming the flats and just thought "low-low-low" in the right places. Faster, more reliable.
Grade 2 introduced natural minor. Grade 3 adds harmonic and (sometimes) melodic.

The leading-tone effect that classical music expects:
A B C D E F G♯ A
That raised 7th creates an augmented 2nd between F and G♯ (3 semitones — a full step + half-step). This gives harmonic minor its Middle-Eastern or Spanish flavour.
Trick: harmonic minor sounds exotic compared to natural minor. Sing both ascending — natural feels "modal/folk", harmonic feels "classical/dramatic". After ten A/B comparisons, your ear locks the difference.

Ascending: A B C D E F♯ G♯ A
Descending: A G F E D C B A
Two different note sets in one scale. Composers chose this in the Baroque to handle melodic lines without the harmonic minor's augmented 2nd "bump".
Grade 3 typically requires melodic minor only on paper; full playing comes Grade 4.

Major · Relative minor · Common form examined
F major · D natural & harmonic minor · Both
B♭ major · G natural & harmonic minor · Both
C major · A natural & harmonic minor · Both
Practise: play the major scale, then immediately its relative minor (natural form). Then play harmonic minor of the same root. Six versions per session.

A new bowing. Notation: slur (curved line) + dot under each note within the slur.
. . . .
♪‿♪‿♪‿♪ = play 4 notes in one bow, but each separated by a tiny pause
The bow stays on the string; the wrist makes a small stop-start motion for each note while moving in one direction.
Where I got stuck: I lifted the bow between notes — that's staccato volante (flying staccato), Grade 6 stuff. Fix: practise on open strings, bow stays on the string, only the wrist pulses. Picture a bow that "hesitates" 4 times in one stroke.

Two unequal notes (often dotted-quaver + semiquaver) on one bow with a tiny stop between them:
♪. 𝅘𝅥𝅯 <-- both on down-bow, stop between them
Used to keep the dotted figure on the same bow direction throughout a phrase. Saves bow-direction confusion.
True shifting (moving the hand to 2nd/3rd/etc. positions) is Grade 4 territory, but Grade 3 introduces the concept and may use one shift in a piece or as a "step out" of 1st position.

Reach higher notes the 1st position can't.
Stay on one string for a phrase (changing tone colour).
Make awkward fingerings easier.

In 3rd position, the 1st finger plays what the 3rd finger plays in 1st position. So on the A string:
1st position: 3rd finger = D5.
3rd position: 1st finger = D5.
The hand moves up the neck by about 1 inch.

On the A string:
Open A, then 3rd finger D (1st position).
Slide the 1st finger up the string until it sounds D.
Now you're in 3rd position. Play 2 (E) and 3 (F♯).
Don't lift; slide smoothly. The thumb travels with the hand.
Trick: the thumb moves at the same time as the fingers. If the thumb stays back, you get a stretched, painful hand. Practise the shift with eyes closed, only feeling the smooth slide. Listen for the slide pitch — at first it'll glissando, later it'll be silent.
Grade 3 may include one piece with a marked shift; Grade 4 requires the technique.

Grade 2 named interval size (2nd, 3rd, etc.). Grade 3 adds quality:
Interval · Semitones · Example (from C)
Perfect 1st (unison) · 0 · C–C
Minor 2nd · 1 · C–D♭
Major 2nd · 2 · C–D
Minor 3rd · 3 · C–E♭
Major 3rd · 4 · C–E
Perfect 4th · 5 · C–F
Tritone (Aug 4 / dim 5) · 6 · C–F♯
Perfect 5th · 7 · C–G
Minor 6th · 8 · C–A♭
Major 6th · 9 · C–A
Minor 7th · 10 · C–B♭
Major 7th · 11 · C–B
Perfect 8ve · 12 · C–C (high)

Perfect: 1st, 4th, 5th, 8ve. Stable, "pure" sound.
Major / minor: 2nd, 3rd, 6th, 7th. Have two flavours.
Tritone: unstable, called diabolus in musica historically.
Trick: the song hooks for intervals — sing the opening and find the interval in it:
Major 2nd: "Happy Birthday" ("-py Birth-")
Minor 3rd: "Greensleeves" ("A-las")
Major 3rd: "When the Saints" ("Oh when")
Perfect 4th: "Here Comes the Bride"
Perfect 5th: "Twinkle, Twinkle" ("-kle, Twin-")
Minor 6th: "The Entertainer" ("ta-ta")
Major 6th: "My Bonnie"
Octave: "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" ("Some-where")
Memorise one song per interval; identify intervals in 1 second.

The Bach Gavottes (both G major and G minor in Suzuki 3) are based on dance forms. Listen to Janine Jansen or Hilary Hahn play any Bach Partita gavotte. Notice how the dance accent (beat 3 of 4/4) is felt rather than punched.

Grade 3 aural expands to:
Sing back a 4–5 note phrase (more contour).
Identify major / minor / chromatic.
Identify key features: same, different, or modified (transposition or change in dynamics).
Clap rhythms with dotted figures.

The examiner plays a note on the piano in a key you haven't been told. You must identify it and play it on the violin. Practise daily for 30 seconds; by Grade 3 exam, you should pick the right string + finger 90% of the time within 5 seconds.

Pitfall · Fix
Low-finger pattern slips back to normal · Drill the low-finger shape on open string mute; visualise the hand position
Confusing harmonic minor (raised 7) with melodic (raised 6+7 up) · Always play them adjacent — A/B compare daily
Slurred staccato becomes lift-staccato · Watch bow hair: must stay on string
Shifting causes glissando in performance · Slow practice with silent shift (lighten thumb during slide)
Tritone identification wrong (called Perfect 4 or 5) · Memorise "Maria" (West Side Story) opening: it's a tritone
Ignoring dotted-rhythm bow distribution · Pencil-mark bow direction + amount for first read
Bow arm tension on B♭ scale · Stop, drop arm to side, shake, restart
